## Why the Sky Is Blue

Sunlight contains all the colors of the visible spectrum, but when it enters Earth's atmosphere, it collides with the tiny gas molecules (mostly nitrogen and oxygen) that are much smaller than the wavelength of light. These molecules scatter the incoming light in all directions through a process called **Rayleigh scattering**. Because shorter wavelengths scatter much more strongly than longer ones, the blue and violet ends of the spectrum are redistributed across the sky, so when you look up (away from the Sun), you see this scattered light coming from every direction. The sky appears blue rather than violet even though violet scatters even more, because the Sun emits less violet light, our eyes are less sensitive to it, and some of it is absorbed higher in the atmosphere.

## Rayleigh Scattering Wavelength Dependence

The intensity of scattered light is inversely proportional to the **fourth power** of the wavelength:

$$I \propto \frac{1}{\lambda^4}$$

This strong wavelength dependence is precisely why blue light (shorter λ, ~450 nm) scatters roughly **5–6 times more** than red light (longer λ, ~650 nm)—which is also the reason sunsets appear red, as the longer path through the atmosphere at dusk removes most of the blue, leaving the transmitted red light.
